agree.reason: The 74-of-112 figure and the measured handling of the inspection make the association hard to dismiss as a few loud people, but the letter offers nothing in return (no meeting, no list of residents needing help), sets no reply date, and drops the dialysis case, so Weller has little pressure or reason to act soon.

honest.reason: The claims stay mostly within the facts, and the wheelchair scenario is clearly hypothetical, but asking for a feasibility study goes beyond what the association actually wants, since it admits management may be right, and 'roughly one day in every eight' is a little generous.

works_the_facts.reason: It works out useful figures (one day in eight, two households in three, the estimate repeated after five months), but it never works out the cost of the outage days to tenants, which would back a rent credit, and it never says how long the repair will take if this pattern continues.

right_comparison.reason: Contrasting the repeated 'six to eight weeks' with the June promise shows the status quo well, but the letter never spells out what the next months look like if nothing changes, such as another August-length outage for the 23 older residents.

qualification.reason: Asking for a due date and 'what you will do if that date passes' is the right kind of checkable condition, but the letter gives no deadline for management's reply and no consequence if it is missed.

objections.reason: It answers the inspection-certificate defence and the claim that only a few residents care, but leaves Weller free to argue the asks are vague, because the stair-climbing chair, trained staff and rent credit are never named and the association offers nothing in return.

fit.reason: It works as an open letter, but at about 470 words it runs over the target, and it leaves out the building, the company, Weller's name and a signature, all of which a lobby posting and a TV station would need.
